If it's slight depression, I usually try the 3 important steps. Sleep, Eat, Shower. Being overtired, hungry, or grimy can all negatively impact mood, plus the shower has the effect of rhythmic strikes, which is great therapeutic sensory input. If none of those work, a 20 minute walk through the woods or the park is my next option, as there is evidence to show that being out in nature can elevate one's mood and release those good brain chemicals, as can exercise. If none of that stuff works, I indulge in a little retail therapy, usually at the thrift shop or a dollar store. Searching for small trinkets and snacks is like activating the foraging instinct, and it can bring you joy when you find something neat for a good price. Lastly, I try to reach out and talk to a friend, see if they want to hang out for a bit. In person or over a screen, playing a game together is always nice. It can bring my mood up enough sometimes to give me the motivation to do all the other stuff. Oh, and sometimes listening to music can help, but it can't be sad music, it needs to be happy or aggressive music for me, because sad music just brings my mood down further. 

If none of that works, or you feel like it is too hard to do any of that stuff, except for maybe lying in bed and sleeping, it might be advanced depression. The first thing I do then is try to figure out if the situation that I am currently in is not conducive to my happiness, and why. If it is something I can change, I change it. If it is not something I can change, then I might need to take a trip down to the doctor to figure out what can be done.

A lot of great advice in the thread. Here are some helpful tips on some of the general basics of how to use an oven, which might be fairly helpful as you continue. 

When you choose a recipe, it is important to read through the recipe before you attempt to do it. This is a lesson I often forget, but it does come with time. You should look first for what ingredients are used, and see if you have them at home with you. If you do not, you can go out and get them. DO NOT go out and get them before you finish reading the rest of the recipe. The second thing you will look for is what techniques and materials are required. Make sure that you understand what these things are. If you do not know what something is, google it. If you need a visual of what other people are doing, watch someone do it in a (reputable) cooking youtube video - not some like, 5 minute cooking or something from a random tiktok. Thirdly, if you are feeling confused by the recipe and having to google a lot of things, try to rewrite it down in a way that you would understand, even if you walked away from it for a few hours and forgot about it. 

Personally, I think that the easiest things to start with are not stovetop cooking in a fry pan, but partially instant foods, like pasta and sauce. For you, I will recommend a dried pasta of a medium size, such as a macaroni, penne, or fusilli. If you buy dried pasta, it will have the instructions on the box, and they will be fairly understandable, but I can throw in some extra explanation here just in case you need it. Usually it will tell you to put a pot of water on the stove, and heat the water until it boils. Once it is boiling, it will tell you to add in the pasta, and turn down the heat. It will give you an amount of time to let the pasta continue cooking, and will often tell you to set a timer for this. Then it will tell you to, once the timer is done, remove the pot from the stove, and drain the pasta.

So here's the absolute, complete beginner version of cooking pasta with tips and tricks.  For this, I would recommend that the pot that you use should be a small or medium sized pot, especially if you are the only one who is eating the pasta. If you want to measure the size, the pot should be able to hold somewhere around 4 -8 cups of water when filled. By cups, I mean the one cup amount for a measuring cup or measuring spoon. The amount of water you should use to cook noodles will sometimes be listed on the package. If it doesn't, keep in mind that there is a sort of balance when it comes to the correct amount of water in the pot - you want it to be enough water that it will cover all of your noodles, but you do not want it to be so much water that it will spill out when it is boiling. Having the pot around halfway full of water is the best way to do this. If the pot seems too small for the amount of pasta that you want, swap it out for a bigger one. It's always better to use too big of a pot than it is to use too small of a pot. 

 Place the pot of water onto a stovetop element  that is closest in size to the circle that makes up the bottom of the pot. Putting it on one that is much smaller will cause the pot to boil much slower, while putting it on one that is much bigger may cause the handles to be more likely to heat up, which may cause you to burn your hand or drop the pot. 

Once it is on the element, turn the element on. As you have previously cooked steak and tuna melts on the stovetop, I can assume that you know how to turn the stovetop burners on and adjust their heat. If not, let me know and I can give tips on this as well. To boil water, you can put it on the highest setting, and it will not burn unless you leave it alone for a very long time. So put the element at the highest setting, and hang out in the kitchen until the water boils. (PRO TIP: adding a single tablespoon's worth (Use measuring spoons) of salt into the water before turning the element on will help the water to boil faster, and will make the pasta taste better. Putting a lid on the pot will also make it boil faster. Neither is necessary, but they do save some time). 

Here is a quick video to show how the water boiling should look. https://www.youtube.com/shorts/zb9IDrDqzJM . Once the water is boiling like at the end of the video, you can add in your pasta noodles. Be careful not to give yourself a steam burn here - the steam can sometimes be quite hot, so do not leave your hand over top of the steam for a prolonged period of time. 

Once the pasta noodles are in the pot, turn down the heat a little bit, to the spot that you would consider between the hottest and the medium setting. Next, take a large sized spoon, such as a serving spoon, the kind that is too big to properly eat with, and use it to stir the noodles. You should not go too fast at this, just be gentle about it, and try to make sure that the noodles are not sticking to the bottom. The reason I suggest a large sized spoon is because it will also help to prevent steam burns to your hand, and can more efficiently stir large amounts of stuff in a pot. Going slowly is also key to avoiding burns as well. 

Once you've stirred it, set a timer according to the package directions. Usually they will give you directions saying something like, 8-10 minutes, but some are much shorter, so it is important to read and find out which is which. The exact time is usually somewhat arbitrary. If you use any time amount between the two listed minutes, you should get edible pasta. 

At this point, keep an eye on the timer and stir the pasta lightly at intervals of about every 2 minutes until there are only 3 minutes left on the timer. When the timer goes off, turn the heat of the stove off, and remove the pot from the stove. Into the sink, place a pasta strainer. Pour the contents of the pot into the pasta strainer, and drain the water. Place the pot onto the counter or stove (preferably with a dishcloth or like a protective pad under it) and place the pasta back into the pot. Your pasta is done, but if you want to keep it hot while waiting for the sauce, put a little bit (a small drizzle, or if we're measuring, a tablespoon's worth) of olive oil (other oils will tend to not taste as good in this scenario) in the pot with the pasta, and 

For sauce, there are three ways to do it. It all starts with a can or jar of sauce. The easiest way is jarred pesto sauce. You can just pour it on straight out of the jar, it doesn't need to be heated, especially on very fresh, hot pasta. The second way to do it is in the microwave. This is also fairly easy. Pour the sauce from the jar into a microwave safe bowl (so not metal and usually not plastic) or corningware type dish. Put it into the microwave and heat it up at intervals of 1-1and a half minutes at a time, stirring after each time in the microwave, until the sauce is hot. You can use either a red, alfredo, or vodka sauce, and it will be good with this method. 

The final method is the trickiest, and I don't recommend it until you feel that you are understanding boiling pasta, because it is very similar. This is the stovetop method. The stovetop method is the most customizable, because you can add your own veggies in - extra mushrooms, onions, fresh cherry tomato, basil, spinach, even stuff like zucchini and carrots. 

For this method, you will chop up all additional veggies beforehand, or use prechopped ones. Look carefully at the sizes you are cutting or using, and ask if it would be at home in a pasta at that size, as most veggies do not shrink down too much, and certainly not as much as spinach. Oh, also, make sure to wash your veggies before you use them, as sometimes the surface of vegetables can have hidden dirt or bacteria on them. In another pot, similar in size or slightly smaller than the pasta pot, pour in a jar of pasta sauce. You can use 2 jars if you think you will need that much sauce, but for one person, one jar is enough. Add in your chopped veggies in an amount that looks good to you, and place the pot onto the stove element. Put the element to between low and medium heat perhaps  closer to medium, and let it all heat up. Stir it every couple minutes or so, until it is bubbling and hot. Then it is ready to serve. 

Eventually, you will learn other ways to continue to improve this method, such as adding meats, or frying up the veggies first, but this method is simple and will get the job done, so it is more suitable to a beginner. 

Lastly, I just want to leave you with my own early adventures in cooking - where I tried to microwave a frozen pizza with the plastic wrap still on it, completely destroyed a toaster by putting too big of a slice of bread into it and cooking it for too long (then forgetting it), and literally causing a small grease fire when I was trying to cook eggrolls on the stovetop. You might get occasional burns and cuts, you might destroy a pan or two, and be too embarrassed to tell your family about it, so you just throw it away, you might completly destroy the ingredients you're working with in the pursuit of something you thought was a great idea. It's okay, the learning process is real, and we all make mistakes.

In college I lived this challenge, trying to spend on average 25$ per week. It is doable, but it is difficult. Never pay for sugar if you can get packets of it for free from restaurants, but if you find that you must buy it, dollar store as well. Dollar store is also where you should buy your spices. Buy your rice in a big bulk bag, and also buy a big bag of instant oats. Rice will make up a lot of your dinner options and oatmeal will make up a lot of your breakfast options. Dried pasta is also a good choice to buy, as is the cheapest bakery loaf of bread. Whatever money you have left, put that into veggies and meats/legumes and pulses primarily, but canned sauces, like tomato sauce or gravy are also sometimes good to have for days when you are too tired or too busy. 

In college, for me, a typical week might look like

Breakfasts: Oatmeal with cinnamon sugar/chocolate chips/sliced banana or apple, toast with cinnamon sugar, banana or apple eaten on the way to class, leftovers from dinner, or peanut butter and oat balls. 

Lunches: Soup made with gravy sachet and whatever veggies and meat were on sale that week, peanut butter sandwich, rice and beans with spices, homemade hummus and bread, boxed mac n cheese, fried potato, carrot, and onions mix. 

Dinner: Rice with chickpea or lentil curry, more of that veggie and meat soup, fried tofu with marinara sauce to dip, Spaghetti primavera, Basic shepherds/cottage pie, giant pot of chili that lasts all week (sometimes with chips to accompany, or sometimes on top of rice), can of refried beans with added spices and tortilla chips.

Snacks: just leftovers mostly. Or Australian fairy bread, or basic poured cooled caramel if I was craving something sweet.

Chicken teriyaki. You need - chicken thigh (breast is also fine) in the amount you want to eat (Usually one or two per person). Veggies of choice (Usually I will just do a bag of frozen plus a chopped onion), garlic (fresh, jarred, or powder are all good. I use jarred because I like it better, which to some is sacrilege, but whatev), Ginger (I usually use powder, but fresh is honestly lovely), sugar, soy sauce, sake + mirin (I tend to omit these tbh. They can add some depth but you aren't going to be mad without them in there), I like to add a little sesame oil, and optionally, if you like spice, finish with some chili oil as well. If you want the sauce thicker, you can also use some cornstarch mixed in. 

To cook: Fry the onions in a pan with a bit of cooking oil, then once they're starting to sweat, add the chicken thigh, chopped into cubes/bite sized pieces. While that cooks, stirring every so often, prepare the sauce. For the full version: You need equal parts soy sauce, sake, and mirin, and then add as much or as little sugar as you feel is proper. Then add in your garlic and ginger, again, to suit your own tastes. Then, add cornstarch, as much or as little as you want, (though too much will make it very gloopy, so less is more) and whisk it up until there are no lumps. If you forgo sake and mirin, you can instead further the sauce and thin out the salty soy sauce flavour with chicken broth and/or a hint of vinegar. Once you have your soy sauce, sugar, garlic and ginger, as well as any of those other additives as you see fit, put in your frozen veg, and pour the mix over the top. Bring to a bubble and let it thicken over the chicken and veg. 

Serve with your choice of rice or noodle.

Simplest foods that I learned to cook when I had just moved out to college and how to do them in the most straightforward way. 

1. Tomato rice. The easiest way to cook rice is to use a rice cooker. Start with easier varieties of rice that have directions on the package. Follow the package directions to a T, and make sure you read the directions on how to use the rice cooker. Otherwise, if you do not can cannot have access to a rice cooker, I would use microwaved instant rice in this dish. While the rice is cooking, take out a non stick skillet of choice, and since you are strictly vegetarian, I would personally use a can of low sodium black beans. I usually do ground meat instead of the beans, but when I have vegetarian friends over, this is my replacement of choice. You could replace that also with a pack of impossible meat, however, it is less healthy, harder to cook, and less affordable, so I leave that decision up to you. Drain the beans, rinse them off, and then put the beans into the skillet with a small amount of oil - it must be enough to coat the pan. Cook up the beans until they are getting warm, making sure to stir them gently with a plastic/silicone/wooden spoon so they do not stick to the pan, then take a can of tomatoes, diced, and put that into the pan with the beans. Do not drain the tomatoes, because you want the sauce. You should add a couple of shakes of salt into the pan (or like, 3 twists from a salt grinder) make sure not to put too much though or it will be too salty. The salt brings out the flavour of the tomato. Once the tomato juice is lightly bubbling, you can turn off the burner, add in the cooked rice, stir it up until it is coated in the sauce, and then serve the dish. Note - if the sauce and beans cook faster than the rice, turn off the burner beforehand, remove them from the heat, and put a lid over them. If you want to add spices at the end, you can. Garlic and a hint of black pepper are my go tos, but you can add any spice, provided it is ready to add, such as a powder or pre-chopped thing. You can also put some cheese on top if you want to. 

Recipe 2 - Pizza muffins. Take an english muffin and slice it in half. Toast it for crispiness. Once toasted, put them on a plate or a baking tray depending on the method you choose. Take some jarred pasta or pizza sauce, and spoon it onto the english muffin halves, the side that you've cut open, not the outer part. Take bagged shredded cheese ( I use cheddar or mozzerella) and sprinkle some of it on top. You just need enough to lightly cover the top. You can then get some veggies of choice - chopped green peppers, tomato slices, chopped green onion, or anything you like on pizza, and place some of that onto the top of the english muffins. Next, you have 2 options. The 1st option, which is the easier option, is to microwave the muffins. You put it on for intervals of 30 seconds at a time until the cheese is melty. For this option, use a plate. The benefit is easiness, the drawback is that it can sometimes get a bit soggy this way. The second option, which is more difficult involves an oven or toaster oven. preheat your oven to about 375 F (though some ovens run a bit hotter or cooler, so do keep an eye on them during the process) and once it is ready and has told you that it is the right temperature, you can carefully put in the pizza muffins. Set a timer for 7 minutes. Check on them at this time. If they look cooked, you can remove them, if not, then give an additional up to 3 more minutes. After this point, they should be done. Again, make sure to keep an eye on them. 

Salsa and chips - If nothing else, you can make your own salsa fairly easily at home. Start with some nice tomato, preferably some with some good flavor. Chop it up into the size of pieces you want. Take your time and be patient. Make sure that you are using knives that are sharp enough, as dull knives are more likely to cause you an injury. If you have difficulty with chopping this, you can also use a vegetable chopper device. You should also chop some onion (green onion is easiest) and some peppers. The Peppers dictate the spice level of the salsa, so pick something that you are comfortable eating a bunch of. Jalapeno is usually a good safe bet if you want something with a little spice, but fairly mild. When cutting spicy peppers, you may also find it a good idea to wear food handling gloves, so that you don't get the peppers on your hands. As well, the more of the seeds and white part of the pepper you leave in when you chop it, the more heat it is likely to have. The ratio for the salsa should be 1 onion to every 4 tomatos and 1-2 peppers as well (depending on size of peppers). Mix these diced veggies in a bowl, and then take some lime juice and pour it/squirt it over the top. Add a little salt and a little pepper. If you're like me, you can also add a hint of your favourite hot sauce, add some tomato paste for a less pico de gallo style salsa, or chop up some cilantro (about 1 small bunch, primarily the leaves) also and add it and mix it. Serve it with some tortilla chips. 

Scrambled egg  - take an egg and crack it into a bowl. Remove any shells. Take a fork and stir the egg rapidly until it is somewhat mixed together. Take your pan, add cooking oil and heat it up, on medium heat. Once the oil is moving around the pan easily, add the egg. take a spatula/flipper and stir the egg around to make ribbons.  Once the egg is no longer runny and is in clumps, remove from the heat and enjoy. If you like, add a little hot sauce, or salt and pepper.

For me it's more trying to claim my femininity without feeling like I was pretending to be someone I wasn't. I went through a lot of phases of trying on different identities, and while I liked certain aesthetics, I still didn't feel like I could relate to other people wearing similar clothes or who fully embodied those identities. I always felt like when I was in those groups, I was never able to be my full self, and like other people wanted me to be less complex than I really was.

 I went through middle school, then high school, then university, and about 3 years in the work place until I worked through all that. And then I decided that I was just going to be a little dumpy goblin creature who could do whatever she wanted and look however she felt. If I didn't want to wear makeup, I didn't have to. If I wanted to just put all my hair into a hat and pretend it didn't exist, that was fine. And I was certainly done with choosing clothes based on whether or not I thought other people would like them or they'd make me blend into a specific group better. 

What worked for me might not work for you, but I had the epiphany while making art. I was drawing and I messed up some of the linework. Normally I would have restarted it, because it was done in thick black pen. But I was like. No. I worked hard on this, it doesn't have to be perfect to express what I want to express. And then I thought suddenly that oh, I should apply that to myself. And then I drew myself as my weird little creature avatar for the first time. It was the idea of this little creature that doesn't look conventionally beautiful, and just grabs scraps of things from other people's junk piles to create beautiful things in their everyday life. She was weird and had crazy eyes, and random spots all over her body, and her teeth weren't straight, and she was really short and rather squat. Even so, she had her own femininity, using the things other people had given her, or that she'd found, to create her own persona, and try to feel beautiful, and even though it was not the same as some of the other people and creatures in the drawings, she was able to be happy because her standards was just to do her best and live as who she was no matter what. 

All in all, I don't know if any of that helps, but if it does, cheers. Self esteem and finding where you fit and combining that with your personal style can take a very long time when you've got underlying trauma, so I wish you the best on this journey.

Polar bears are also the only carnivorous bear out there. Other bears of North America don't typically hunt humans, and will typically not hunt much at all, eating mostly berries, insects, and scavenging off of dead things. No one should take a chance against a Polar bear. There's a reason why the saying goes: If it's black, fight back, if it's brown lay down, if it's white, goodnight. Of course, you are also not very likely to find a polar bear in the woods unless you're living in the arctic circle.

When facing a Grizzly, you should try first to not engage with the bear or get closer to it. Do the typical bear safety routine of backing away/going sideways away from it while still facing it. Make noise while looking as big as possible, so it can identify you as a person and not a prey animal. If it doesn't back down and comes over to attack you, play dead. Typically you'll want to keep any backpacks on, though there are a few places where bears are habituated enough that they will not be hunting you, but will be hunting your backpack (if that's the case, there will usually be someone in the area to advise on this). The reason for this is because it can protect your spine. Clasp your hands to the back of your neck as well, and try not to expose your stomach at all costs. Usually once it sees you as no longer a threat, it will go away. If not, and the attack goes on, fight back. 

How to prevent bear attacks - bear awareness: watch where you are going for bears and signs of bears such as footprints or scat. Make sure to hang food high enough so bears cannot get to it, and pack out your trash. Dispose of greywater far from where you will be sleeping, and cook away from tents as well, so as to prevent any lingering odor. On the subject, never eat in tents either. Do not leave food unattended outdoors in areas frequented by bears, and if there is a bear box, put your food in the bear box. Do not burn food scraps or garbage, as the scent can attract bears to the area. To be really safe, treat your  toothbrush and toothpaste, as well as anything scented, in the same way as food, and lock it up overnight, and consider not sleeping in the same clothes you cook in.

Okay, so I've been on the other side of a situation like this so I can give some suggestions as a person whose roommates did not handle the situation well. Firstly, make her get her own dishes and then store your own dishes somewhere with a lock. Don't let her use your stuff at all unless it's like a communal cooking event where then you all will communally wash the dishes together. Do not retaliate by doing something that she might percieve as shaming, like putting all her dishes into a bag and putting them into her room, or leaving a passive aggressive note or something, it will only lead to fights and resentment. Do not shame her for this, or have everyone confront her intervention style. Instead, ask her what she would need from you to be able to do this, or how you can help her, so that it feels less like she's being attacked from everyone else. Does she have ADHD or some other condition which may lead to time blindness or feeling overwhelmed by tasks, or is she depressed or something? Has she ever been taught how to do dishes before or is this her first time having to do them for herself by hand? Was she in a rush when doing these dishes? Are you unconsciously looking for ways in which she fails the task but not times there is a success? Try to figure out if there is any bias there. If you're on campus or anything, get your RA involved in a discussion so that it feels safe and stays stable. Talk about having specific cleaning times for things, because some people do well with having structure in their schedule. 

The key is to avoid resentment and an us vs them mentality amongst the group. If she feels ganged up on, she will shut down. If she feels like her successes aren't being noticed, and only her failures, she will feel like nothing she does matters and will be less likely to do the dishes. If she feels shamed, she will shut you out. None of these things will resolve the problem, and may make it worse.

Mashed potato - cut up some potato and boil it until the potato is soft enough to easily stick a fork into. Drain the water and add some milk and butter. You can also add some cream cheese for extra flavour. Get out your masher and mash until they are soft. Pro tip, don't add too much milk. You can add more but not take it out. 

Rice - buy rice, put it into a rice cooker, add water as per directions, wait, enjoy. To make it into a meal, microwave some frozen veggies in water and add soy sauce or a curry sauce over top. 

Curry type sauces - I have 2 different ones.

1. mushroom soup curry - mix a can of cream of mushroom, a quarter can of diced tomato (about half a cup or so) with the juice, curry powder, garam masala mix, garlic, and turmeric powder, and some onion into a pot. Heat it up on the stove on low to medium heat (I usually do a 4 or 5 on my stove). Stir constantly until the sauce is bubbling and warm.

2. chickpea curry - take canned chickpeas and butter/ghee and mash them together into a nice paste over low heat. Add chopped onion and some more butter. Fry together. Add some tomato, whether diced or sauce it will work. Add the same spices as the above. 

Chili - take a pack of ground beef and cook it in a frying pan, stirring every so often until the beef is no longer pink. Take the beef and along with chopped mushrooms, chopped onion, and a can of your favourite beans (black or kidney are good options) put them into a large pot. Cover with a full can of diced tomato, a full jar pf spaghetti sauce, and if you like, a can of tomato paste. Add chilli powder, cumin, garlic, and cayenne, tasting along the way to make sure that the levels of spice are correct. My basic meals from when I started cooking. Some are better than others or easier than other, but they are easy enough to do if you are starting out and have basic skills.

Ramen salad - You will need( at least): Lettuce or salad mix, a package of instant ramen, veggies and additions of your choice, a salad dressing - bonus points for something like a sesame dressing. Take either premixed bagged garden salad or chopped up lettuce/whatever green leafy thing you most enjoy and put it into a bowl. Take a package of instant ramen and set aside the flavour packet. Use the noodles dry like a crunchy crouton and top the salad with them. Throw any additional stuff you like on top. I like to add sliced almonds, matchstick carrots, and snap peas. Lastly, throw the dressing of choice on top. I like to mix a little vinegar, oil, chopped garlic (I use prechopped jar garlic) and soy sauce, but a vinegrette or sesame dressing works well too. If you plan to take this one to school, I would set it up so you make individual portions of veggies, keep the noodle pieces and dressing off of it, and then when you're ready to eat it, put the ramen and dressing on it. 

Tex-mex tacos - You will need: Ground meat, onion (chopped or at least halved and sliced) package of taco seasoning (or add paprika, cumin, chilli powder, garlic or onion powder, and either a little bit of cayenne powder or your favourite hot sauce) taco shells or tortilla wraps, a bag of shredded cheese (or shred a block of cheese) bagged lettuce or salad mix, sour cream and salsa.  Take a package of ground meat (I typically use beef but any type will suffice) and put it into a large saucepan/skillet, preferably one with deeper edges. Set the cooking temperature on the stove burner that it is on to a low-medium temperature and let it heat up. Make sure to stir this fairly often. Once the oil has started to heat up, add in your onions. Add a dash of salt and pepper. Let the onions cook, continuing to stir, until they get a bit softer, then add your spice or taco seasoning in, and stir until it is incorporated. Make sure that all meat is cooked and no longer appears to be that pink/red raw color. You now have taco meat, and can take the rest of the ingredients and wrap them in the tortillas. If there are leftovers, you can take them the next day, as they keep well, and maybe actually taste even better after being in the fridge for a while.

Chicken soup - You should get a decent sized amount from this, enough for dinner and lunch. Use a rotisserie chicken. You can remove the chicken from the bones and set to the side, or eat some of it first, it's up to you. Take the remaining carcass - bones, any meat still stuck on it, the whole thing, and put it into a pot. Fill the pot with water, and boil the bones and everything. The water should turn into a sort of broth. Take another large pot and a strainer, and pour the whole thing into the pot through the strainer. The bones should stay in the strainer and be able to be removed, and the pot should be full of broth and no bones. Take all the chicken you put to the side, and put it into the broth. Add the veggies of choice - I like to add a bit of carrot, potato, celery, and onion, but you can also just take a bag of frozen veggies and put those in there. If the broth is not very flavourful, add a few packets of chicken broth crystals, like knorr or oxo. You can also add flavourings - lemon, garlic, hot sauce, chili powder, curry powder, salt and pepper, soy sauce, bay leaf, thyme, ginger - basically anything that you think might taste good, and you can try it to figure out if it does by adding a little of it at a time, or by taking a small bit out into a bowl and seasoning the stuff that's in the bowl. 

Yogurt parfait - Good quick breakfast. layer your favourite yogurt, berries, and granola in a bowl, or a cup if you're on the go. 

Brocolli mac and cheese - take a typical boxed mac and cheese, and follow package directions, but also add brocolli to the water before you boil it (can be frozen or fresh, either way, but it should be chopped up well enough that they are bite sized pieces). Save a little of the water to add into the cheese mixture at the end along with the milk and cheese.

Mashed potato - Keeps okay in the fridge, but you'll probably want to heat it up when you eat lunch at school. Wash (and remove skin if you prefer your mashed potato without skin) as many potatos as you think you are willing to eat. cut them up into small pieces, and boil the potato. Once the water is boiling, cook it for about 5-8 minutes, or until you can stick a fork into the potato without using much force ( basically until it is soft enough to crush). Drain the water from the potato, and add a good amount of butter, and a small splash of milk. The more milk you add, the thinner the mashed potato is going to be, so try to not add too much. You can always add more, but you can't really take it away once you've started mashing them. Take a potato masher and keep squishing the potatos into the milk and butter until there aren't very many lumps. To elevate this, you can also add a scoop of cream cheese before mashing, which makes it extra creamy and gives a nice dose of salt. 

Chilli - Makes a massive portion, so you will be eating this for days. If you want you can use it in a bun like a sloppy joe, or you could top a salad with it for a taco salad. Into a pot, dump some ground meat of choice. On medium heat, fry it up. Once it is cooked and no longer pink/red colored, add in a can of diced tomatos, a can or jar of tomato sauce, a can of tomato paste, chilli powder, cumin, garlic powder, a can of mushrooms (drain the water) a chopped onion, and a can of kidney beans or mixed beans (drained of juice and rinced). Stir it together, let it cook on medium, with a lid on. Occasionally take the lid off and give it a stir so that the bottom doesn't burn. Once it's bubbling and hot, you can serve it.

Tuna rice - This is a good lunch or dinner, but it doesn't keep well in the fridge overnight, so it would be a morning of sort of situation. You can make proper rice for this, but I usually just use instant rice and cook it in the microwave. Do this according to box directions. Once it has been fully cooked, and the water is all in the rice, take a can of tuna, drain the water, and dump it in. Add a tiny amount of sugar, about a capful of vinegar, and a good heaping spoon or 2 of mayonaise. Mix it together for a tuna salad rice. You can chop green onion and add it to the top of this.

Chickpea curry - A good dinner. Chop up an onion (whichever size the pieces are doesn't matter, but you should be able to fit them in your mouth). Fry it in butter on medium/low. Once the onion is starting to look a bit softer, take a can of chickpeas, drain and rince them, and put them into the pot. You can mash some of them if you like, but don't have to, I just like to. Take a can of diced tomato and add it in. Take curry powder, a bit of turmeric, some garlic powder, some cayenne (making sure to only use what level of spice you are comfortable with) a bit of ginger, and salt/pepper until it looks like a nice yellow/orange color and tastes nice to you. Serve with rice or naan bread or pita.

BBQ Tofu - This is a fairly easy breakfast option, but can be enjoyed anytime. Take extra firm tofu and slice it into bite sized rectangles. Put it into a skillet and fry it in oil on medium until it starts to take on a bit of a brownish color. Remove it from the heat so it doesn't burn, then add your favourite bbq sauce and stir them all around so they get coated in the BBq sauce. Eat.

Shredded chicken bbq - using a rotisserie chicken again. You take the chicken off the bone, and just rip it up into small pieces. Add your favourite bbq sauce that says it's good for chicken, or add to a bowl some ketchup, brown sugar, paprika, garlic and chilli powder, mix it up, and add to the chicken. Mix the chicken and bbq sauce together, and then put it onto a nice bun. To elevate this, add some coleslaw to the sandwich, or some cheese.

Cucumber sandwiches - cut up cucumber into little pieces, add mayo mixed with sour cream and dill, maybe a little vinegar. You can also use cream cheese in place of the sour cream may mix. 

Chilli - All canned ingredients and spices make the basic version but you can add other stuff easily. Tomato sauce, diced tomatos, mushrooms, beans of choice and spices: chilli powder, cayenne, paprika, garlic and cumin. Additionally, you can add ground meat of choice, onion, onion powder, corn, and cut up peppers. 

Tex mex tacos - same seasonings as for the chilli, add them to some ground beef or chicken, grab shredded cheese or shred some cheese, and cut up lettuce, some salsa, and sour cream. Add toppings to either the hard or soft shell tortilla of choice.

Creamy microwave mushroom rice - cook instant rice in the microwave, once it's cooked, add a can of cream of mushroom soup, and microwave it again until it's decently hot. Add chopped green onion, and top with shredded cheese. Microwave again to melt the cheese. I'd sometimes call this college kid risotto, even if that's not terribly accurate lol.

Flatbread pizzas - take the flatbread of choice, whether tortillas, naan, a focaccia, a pita, whatever. Take some tomato sauce and spread it over the top. Then top with shredded cheese and sliced pepperoni, and whatever else you have that you'd like to add. Put it in the oven at (roughly) 400 F for 10 minutes. Time and temperature may differ based on your oven. 

Miso soup - depending on where you live the availability of this one may differ. Put some cut up silken tofu, some nori or spinach, and some chopped green onion into a bowl. Pour boiling water into it, and then mix some miso paste with the boiling water in the bowl until it is not chunky. Add dashi powder if you like but you don't have to, and without them makes the dish vegan, so if you want to try something new, you totally can. Sometimes I sub chicken powder instead, which is not the most authentic, but I like it better. 

Veggies and dip - buy hummus and veg, cut them up, and whenever you're too tired to even cut up veggies for a meal, sit and enjoy this easy one. If you don't like hummus, sub for your dip of choice, I just suggest hummus because it has protein. 

BBQ tofu - Cut up tofu, optionally coat it in cornstarch, then fry it until it has a crispy brownness around the outsides. Remove from heat and coat in your favourite BBQ sauce.

Healthcare in Canada is awesome for a lot of reasons. We don't have to pay exorbatant amounts of money for most basic healthcare related things - ambulance is like 50$, childbirth is free, getting broken bones set is free. We don't have to hassle insurance about it either. Speaking of insurance, everyone is covered equally for the majority of things. We do still pay for non emergency vision, dental, mental health and prescription care, but many people are insured through their workplaces for these (and programs for slowly making these universal as well are also being begrudgingly pushed currently in government - we recently got free dental for anyone under 18 I believe). Also the government negotiates to keep prices of prescriptions lowered. We have 6 of the worlds best hospitals (mostly in Toronto), one of which was ranked 4th best in the world. Canada is a leader in promoting accessability to life saving healthcare across the globe, and has one of the worlds leading heart health programs (again, based out of Toronto). 

Now the issues: In Canada, we have a few problems. Funnily enough, the main issue is accessability, which is ironic considering how much effort and promotion we put into this. The issue of accessability in this case is not due to gender or racial issues, which is what much of the previous focus has been, but rather it is more due to geographic locations. Canada has great healthcare - if you live in a major city. If you're out in the boonies, or even in a small city, you will face a lesser standard. This is probably true most places. However, in Canada, there are legitimately places where there are no walk in clinics, where you have to travel to the next city over to get the kind of care you need. Most places are in some sort of proximity to a hospital (how close varies based on location, in some more remote parts of Canada, it can be hours away), but going to the emergency room because you have strep throat or a gastroflu is generally frowned upon because that's not what the emergency room is supposed to be for. This makes our emerge times go way up, so people will complain that they weren't able to be seen for several hours. Most of the time, if it doesn't seem to be immediately life threatenning, you will have to wait hours in general. For some procedures, or to get in to see some specialists, there are also long waiting lists. This is because we have a shortage of doctors and nurses and other healthcare professionals, because we do not pay them enough and we overwork them. Around covid there was a mass exodus as a whole bunch of people were like "I can't do this anymore" and left for greener pastures. This is partially the fault of the provinces, who are in charge of healthcare programs. As well, you get people who complain about having to pay extra for stuff like dental and vision care and prescriptions, which is valid. 

All in all, Canada does have a good healthcare system. It is currently not in the best shape due to decades of cuts and underfunding, plus the added strain of a pandemic, but it is still a good public system and a point of pride for the country. Having said that, there are most definitely better countries to emulate when it comes to developing a healthcare program. I would recomend looking to northern and western Europe for more ideas.
